questions.stem: The role of marketing management is best described as:
options: obtaining and allocating the funds the business needs for its day-to-day operations
recruiting, developing and rewarding the employees who deliver the product to customers
planning and controlling how the business identifies and meets customer needs profitably
organising the transformation of inputs into finished goods and services at the lowest cost
questions.explanation: Marketing management plans, implements and monitors activities that identify customer needs and satisfy them at a profit. Transforming inputs is operations, funding is finance and staffing is human resources.

questions.stem: A new Newcastle sparkling water brand sets the goal: 'Within 12 months, 40% of 18-30 year olds in the Hunter will recognise our brand.' Which marketing objective is this?
options: profit margin
market coverage
customer awareness
sales growth
questions.explanation: Recognition of the brand by the target market is a customer awareness objective, typical of a new product. Sales growth targets the change in sales, and profit margin targets profit as a share of revenue.

questions.stem: A clothing retailer's sales rise from $400,000 to $460,000 over a year. Its marketing objective was 10% sales growth. Which statement is correct?
options: sales grew by 60%, so the objective was exceeded
sales grew by 15%, so the objective was exceeded
sales grew by 13%, so the objective was exceeded
sales grew by 6%, so the objective was not met
questions.explanation: Sales growth = (460,000 - 400,000) / 400,000 x 100 = 15%, above the 10% target. Dividing the increase by the new sales figure gives about 13%, which uses the wrong base.

questions.stem: Market segmentation is the process of:
options: setting different prices for a product according to its cost of production
dividing the business into separate departments for marketing, finance and operations
dividing a market into groups of customers with similar needs or characteristics
deciding which wholesalers and retailers will carry the business's products
questions.explanation: Segmentation splits a market into groups whose members share needs, characteristics or behaviour, so the business can choose which to target. Choosing intermediaries is a place decision.

questions.stem: A gym in Parramatta targets people who value an active lifestyle and see fitness as part of their identity. This is segmentation by:
options: behavioural factors
psychographic factors
demographic factors
geographic factors
questions.explanation: Psychographic segmentation groups customers by lifestyle, values, attitudes and personality. Demographic segmentation uses measurable characteristics such as age, income and gender.

questions.stem: An airline offers rewards to customers who fly with it more than ten times a year. Which type of segmentation does this use?
options: geographic, based on the region where customers live
behavioural, based on how often customers use the product
psychographic, based on customers' values and personality
demographic, based on customers' age, gender and income
questions.explanation: Behavioural segmentation groups customers by how they use or respond to a product: usage rate, loyalty, benefits sought or occasion. Frequent flyers are a usage-rate segment.

questions.stem: A business that sells one product with the same marketing mix to the whole market is using:
options: behavioural segmentation
undifferentiated targeting
differentiated targeting
concentrated targeting
questions.explanation: Undifferentiated, or mass, targeting ignores segment differences and uses one mix for everyone, as with basic staples such as salt. Differentiated targeting uses separate mixes for several segments.

questions.stem: A Wollongong surfboard maker sells only high-performance boards to competitive surfers. Which targeting strategy is this, and what is its main risk?
options: differentiated targeting; it needs separate mixes for many segments
undifferentiated targeting; it ignores differences between customers
concentrated targeting; it spreads its resources over too many markets
concentrated targeting; it depends heavily on one small segment
questions.explanation: Focusing on one segment is concentrated targeting, which builds specialist expertise but leaves the business exposed if that segment shrinks. Running separate mixes for several segments is differentiated targeting.

questions.stem: Positioning refers to:
options: the place a product occupies in customers' minds compared with competitors
the physical location of a product on a supermarket shelf or in a catalogue
the ranking of a business by sales revenue within its industry
the position of the marketing manager in the organisation chart
questions.explanation: Positioning is how customers perceive a product relative to competing products, for example as premium, value or eco-friendly. Shelf location is part of place and promotion, not positioning itself.

questions.stem: A skincare brand wants to be positioned as a luxury product. Which marketing mix decision would most undermine this positioning?
options: setting a price well above that of mass-market skincare brands
selling it in discount bins at every supermarket and petrol station
selling it only through department stores and the brand's own website
packaging it in heavy glass jars with minimal, elegant labelling
questions.explanation: Positioning must be supported by every element of the mix. Intensive discount distribution signals a cheap, everyday product and conflicts with a luxury image, whereas selective outlets, premium packaging and high prices reinforce it.

questions.stem: Before launching a new plant-based pie, a Sydney bakery runs taste tests with 200 customers and refines the recipe. This shows the role of market research in:
options: replacing the need to promote the new product
reducing the risk that a new product will fail
guaranteeing that the new product will succeed
setting the legal minimum price of the product
questions.explanation: Research during new product development tests ideas, prototypes and prices with real customers so problems are fixed before launch, lowering the risk of failure. Research reduces risk but cannot guarantee success.

questions.stem: Which are all product attributes?
options: skimming, penetration and markdowns
features, packaging and branding
advertising, publicity and discounts
wholesalers, retailers and agents
questions.explanation: Product attributes are what make up the product itself: its features, packaging and brand. Advertising and discounts are promotion, intermediaries are place, and skimming and markdowns are pricing.

questions.stem: A Dubbo accounting firm trains staff to explain advice in plain language, introduces online booking and renovates its reception area. These improve the service through:
options: price, place and promotion
features, packaging and branding
advertising, selling and publicity
people, processes and physical evidence
questions.explanation: Because services are intangible, customers judge them by the staff (people), the way the service is delivered (processes) and the tangible surroundings (physical evidence). Price, place and promotion are other parts of the mix.

questions.stem: A sports drink brand releases the same drink in two new flavours. This is a:
options: brand extension
new product category
markdown strategy
line extension
questions.explanation: A line extension adds new versions, such as flavours or sizes, within an existing product line under the same brand. A brand extension uses the brand name in a different product category.

questions.stem: A well-known sunscreen brand launches its own range of sunglasses under the same name. Which is the main disadvantage of this brand extension?
options: launching the range costs much more than building a completely new brand from nothing
a brand extension always reduces sales of the original sunscreen range
a failure in the new category could damage the reputation of the original brand
customers will not recognise the brand name on the new range of sunglasses
questions.explanation: Brand extensions use existing awareness and trust to cut launch costs, but a poor product in the new category can harm the parent brand. Recognition of the name is the main advantage, not a problem.

questions.stem: In which stage of the product life cycle are sales rising quickly and new competitors entering the market?
options: maturity
decline
growth
introduction
questions.explanation: In the growth stage, sales and profits rise rapidly and competitors are attracted. In maturity, sales level off and competition is at its most intense.

questions.stem: A product's sales have levelled off and competition is intense. Which marketing response is most typical of this stage?
options: using price skimming to recover development costs quickly
defending market share with promotion, price offers and product updates
building initial awareness with heavy advertising to early adopters
withdrawing all promotion and preparing to remove the product
questions.explanation: In maturity, businesses defend share and try to extend the life cycle with promotion, competitive pricing and modifications. Building first awareness and skimming belong to introduction.

questions.stem: A Bathurst furniture maker's cost per chair is $40 and it adds a 25% mark-up. Using cost-plus pricing, what is the selling price?
questions.explanation: Cost-plus price = cost x (1 + mark-up) = $40 x 1.25 = $50. Cost-plus is simple and covers costs, but it ignores what customers will pay and competitors' prices.

questions.stem: A games console is launched at a high price, which is lowered over time as competitors enter. This pricing method is:
options: cost-plus pricing
price skimming
penetration pricing
competitive pricing
questions.explanation: Skimming sets a high initial price to earn high margins from early adopters willing to pay more, then reduces it. Penetration pricing does the opposite, starting low to win share quickly.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of penetration pricing?
options: high prices that discourage most customers from trying the product
slow growth in market share while competitors enter the market
a premium image that is hard to change once it is established
low early margins, and customers may resist later price rises
questions.explanation: Penetration pricing builds share quickly with a low price, but margins are thin and raising prices later can drive customers away. High prices and a premium image belong to skimming.

questions.stem: A rideshare app raises fares during storms and on New Year's Eve and lowers them in quiet periods. Which statement best evaluates this pricing method?
options: it sets every price at cost plus a fixed mark-up, so profit per trip never changes
it keeps prices fixed all year round, so customers can easily plan the cost of each trip
it sets prices just below rivals' prices, so the app never earns a premium margin
it matches price to demand to earn more, but customers may see peak prices as unfair
questions.explanation: Dynamic pricing changes prices in real time with demand, increasing revenue and smoothing demand, but it can damage goodwill if customers feel exploited. Cost-plus and competitive pricing do not respond to demand in this way.

questions.stem: A designer jacket normally priced at $120 is marked down by 30% at the end of winter. What is its new price, and why use a markdown?
options: $84, to clear seasonal stock before it loses value
$90, to raise the profit margin on each jacket sold
$36, to sell the jacket below the cost of making it
$84, to increase the perceived quality of the brand
questions.explanation: New price = $120 x (1 - 0.30) = $84. Markdowns clear slow-moving or seasonal stock and free up cash and space, but frequent markdowns can train customers to wait for sales and weaken brand image.

questions.stem: A software firm sets the price of its farm management app at $2,000 a year because it saves the average farm about $10,000 in labour, even though it costs little to supply. This is:
options: value-based pricing, set on the benefit customers receive
cost-plus pricing, set on the cost of supplying each customer
competitive pricing, set at the level of the market leader
penetration pricing, set low to win market share quickly
questions.explanation: Value-based pricing sets the price according to the value customers perceive, here the savings the app delivers, which can earn high margins. Its limitation is that perceived value is hard to measure accurately.

questions.stem: A Mudgee winery sells some wine directly to visitors at its cellar door and some through bottle shops. Which is an advantage of the cellar door channel?
options: the winery passes all storage and selling costs to retailers
the winery keeps the full margin and controls the customer experience
the winery reaches far more customers across Australia at once
the winery no longer needs to spend anything on promotion
questions.explanation: Direct channels remove intermediaries, so the producer keeps their margin and controls service and presentation. Indirect channels through retailers give much wider reach and share selling costs.

questions.stem: Selling a product through as many outlets as possible, such as supermarkets, petrol stations and convenience stores, is called:
options: intensive market coverage
selective market coverage
exclusive market coverage
concentrated targeting
questions.explanation: Intensive coverage suits low-cost, frequently bought products such as soft drinks and snacks. Selective uses a limited number of outlets, and exclusive uses one outlet per area.

questions.stem: A prestige watch brand sells through only one authorised dealer in each Australian capital city. Which is a disadvantage of this level of market coverage?
options: dealers have little reason to give the brand strong service and support
limited availability may lose sales to customers who cannot reach a dealer
the brand loses control over how its watches are displayed, serviced and sold
the high number of outlets weakens the brand's exclusive image
questions.explanation: Exclusive coverage protects a prestige image and gives close control over dealers, who are motivated by their sole rights, but it restricts availability. Loss of control and image dilution are risks of intensive coverage.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of online distribution compared with in-store distribution?
options: the business must pay rent on a shop in every suburb it serves
customers can shop only during the store's opening hours
customers cannot see, touch or try the product before buying it
the business can reach customers only within its local area
questions.explanation: Online selling offers wide reach, 24-hour access and lower premises costs, but customers cannot inspect products, and delivery and returns add cost. Local reach and opening hours are limitations of stores.

questions.stem: A breakfast cereal maker gives supermarkets a discount for prominent shelf space and also runs TV advertising aimed at families. These promotions are aimed respectively at:
options: intermediaries in both cases
end customers in both cases
intermediaries, then end customers
end customers, then intermediaries
questions.explanation: Trade discounts for shelf space push the product through intermediaries, while TV advertising pulls demand from end customers, who then seek the product in stores. Many businesses combine both.

questions.stem: Which element of the promotion mix suits a business selling complex industrial equipment to a small number of large buyers?
options: opinion leaders
personal selling
mass advertising
sales promotions
questions.explanation: Personal selling allows two-way communication, product demonstrations and tailored solutions, which suit complex, high-value products and few buyers. Its limitation is the high cost per customer reached.

questions.stem: A Sydney charity event gains free coverage on the evening news after a business issues a media release. Which is the main limitation of this public relations activity?
options: the coverage costs far more than paid television advertising
audiences trust news coverage less than paid advertisements
the coverage can only be used to promote a sales discount
the business cannot control what the media reports or when
questions.explanation: Publicity is low-cost and seen as credible because it comes from an independent source, but the business has no control over the message or timing. Audiences generally trust news more than advertising.

questions.stem: A cosmetics start-up pays a popular social media creator to review its products for her 500,000 followers. Which statement best evaluates this promotion?
options: it is a sales promotion, because it offers followers a temporary price discount
it is personal selling, because the creator meets each follower face to face
it uses an opinion leader's credibility to reach a target audience, but her conduct can affect the brand
it guarantees sales, because followers are obliged to buy any product the creator reviews and recommends
questions.explanation: Opinion leaders and influencers can reach a defined audience with a trusted voice, but the brand depends on their reputation, and paid posts must be disclosed as advertising to avoid misleading consumers. No promotion guarantees sales.

questions.stem: The federal government raises the excise duty on alcohol. What is the most likely effect on a Hunter Valley winery's marketing?
options: higher costs may force price rises, reducing demand for its products
lower costs allow the winery to cut prices and increase sales
the winery must stop all advertising of its alcoholic products
the winery can claim a subsidy to cover its marketing costs
questions.explanation: Excise duties are taxes on goods such as alcohol, tobacco and fuel, so higher excise raises costs and usually prices. Government procurement and subsidies are other political influences, which can increase demand or lower costs.

questions.stem: During a recession, a car dealer finds customers delaying purchases. Which marketing response best suits this phase of the business cycle?
options: launching its most expensive models with price skimming
promoting value, finance offers and lower-priced models
raising prices to signal that its cars are exclusive
cutting all promotion until the economy fully recovers
questions.explanation: In a downturn, incomes and confidence fall, so marketers stress value, offer finance and promote cheaper lines. Raising prices or skimming would deter cautious buyers.

questions.stem: A retailer uses an AI tool to analyse customers' purchase histories and target them with personalised offers. Which is the most important ethical consideration?
options: making sure the AI tool is cheaper than employing marketing staff to do the work
using the data to charge the highest price each customer is likely to accept
selling the customer data to other businesses to cover the cost of the tool
collecting and using customer data with consent, transparency and secure storage
questions.explanation: AI makes personalised marketing efficient, but businesses must be transparent, obtain consent, protect data and avoid unfair or discriminatory targeting; the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) also regulates how personal information is handled. Exploiting or selling data without consent is unethical.

questions.stem: Under the Australian Consumer Law, a business must not engage in conduct in trade or commerce that is:
options: more expensive than the prices charged by its competitors
aimed at a particular segment rather than at the whole market
different from the conduct of the market leader in its industry
misleading or deceptive, or likely to mislead or deceive
questions.explanation: The Australian Consumer Law prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct in trade or commerce, including false advertising claims about price, quality or origin. Charging more than rivals or targeting a segment is lawful.

questions.stem: A customer's new $900 washing machine floods her laundry on its first use. The retailer says she must deal with the manufacturer. Under the consumer guarantees, which statement is correct?
options: she is entitled to a remedy only if she bought an extended warranty at the time
she must accept a repair, because businesses always choose the remedy for any failure
the retailer must provide a remedy, and for a major failure she can choose a refund or replacement
the retailer has no duty, because only the manufacturer gives guarantees on goods
questions.explanation: Consumer guarantees, such as acceptable quality, apply automatically, and the retailer must provide a remedy; for a major failure the consumer can choose a refund or replacement. Businesses cannot exclude the guarantees, and an extended warranty is not needed.

questions.stem: A Sydney juice company's sales are $2.4 million in a market worth $16 million. Its target market share is 18%. Which statement is correct?
options: its market share is 6.7%, which is below its target
its market share is 20%, which is above its target
its market share is 15%, which is below its target
its market share is 18%, which meets its target
questions.explanation: Market share = 2.4 / 16 x 100 = 15%, three percentage points short of the 18% target. Dividing the market by the company's sales gives 6.7, which is not a share.

questions.stem: A campaign costing $12,000 attracts 300 new customers. The business's target customer acquisition cost is $50. Which is the correct conclusion?
options: the cost per new customer is $40, so the campaign beat its target
the cost per new customer is $60, so the campaign missed its target
the cost per new customer is $25, so the campaign beat its target
the cost per new customer is $400, so the campaign missed its target
questions.explanation: Customer acquisition cost = $12,000 / 300 = $40, below the $50 target, so the campaign was cost-effective. Comparing metrics with targets, past results and industry benchmarks shows where corrective action is needed.

questions.stem: A bakery chain's market share falls from 18% to 15% while the industry is growing. Research shows customers rate its products well but find few of its stores convenient. Which corrective action best targets the problem?
options: redesign its products, since customers dislike the current range
reduce advertising, since product quality is already rated well
expand distribution through more outlets or online ordering and delivery
cut prices on all products to match the cheapest competitor in each local area
questions.explanation: Corrective action should address the cause shown by the data: the weakness is place, not product or price. Cutting prices would reduce margins without fixing access, and redesigning well-rated products targets the wrong element.

questions.stem: A marketing team runs a sales promotion that doubles demand for a product, but operations cannot produce enough and many orders are cancelled. What does this best show?
options: demand should never be increased once a product is in growth
marketing decisions must be aligned with operations capacity and plans
sales promotions are always ineffective at increasing demand
the operations function should set all of the marketing objectives itself
questions.explanation: Marketing is interdependent with other functions: a campaign must fit production capacity, finance and staffing, or it creates unmet demand and disappointed customers. The promotion worked; the failure was in coordination.
